Published in final edited form as: Curr Pain Headache Rep. 2013 Oct;17(10):10.1007/s11916-013-0370-7. doi: 10.1007/s11916-013-0370-7 Abstract The influence of environmental factors on the clinical manifestation of migraine has been a matter of extensive debate over the past decades. Migraineurs commonly report foods, alcohol, meteorologic or atmospheric changes, exposure to light, sounds, or odors, as factors that trigger or aggravate their migraine attacks. In the same way, physicians frequently follow this belief in their recommendations in how migraineurs may reduce their attack frequency, especially with regard to the consumption of certain food components. Interestingly, despite being such a common belief, most of the clinical studies have shown conflicting results. The aim of the review is to critically analyze clinical and pathophysiological facts that support or refute a correlation between certain environmental stimuli and the occurrence of migraine attacks. Given the substantial discrepancy between patients' reports and objective clinical data, the methodological difficulties of investigating the link between environmental factors and migraine are highlighted. Keywords: Migraine, Trigger, Environmental Stimuli, Headache, Precipitant INTRODUCTION From a clinical perspective, it seems to be quite clear that environmental factors influence the course of the clinical picture in migraineurs. Patients commonly report that certain external factors such as meteorological changes [1–6] or specific food components [5, 6] can influence the initiation or aggravate an ongoing migraine attack. An important caveat to consider is the difficulty to reliably identify migraine triggers. Two recent publications addressing headache triggers and causality concluded that natural experimentation is not a reliable method for individuals to identify migraine triggers [7, 8]. The authors proposed that formal experimentation or diary studies using advanced statistical modeling techniques may be necessary to assign causation to headache triggers [7, 8]. Therefore, we may not be equipped to correctly identify migraine triggers in clinical practice. This is an important question for diagnostic and therapeutic reasons. Schurks et al. have recently proposed that precipitating factors are important in the characterization of the migraine phenotype despite not being included in the current diagnostic criteria of headache disorders [9]. Moreover, there is significant controversy regarding what the therapeutic implications are [10]. From a pathophysiologic point of view, patients' reports suggest that these external stimuli may have an effect on the susceptible brain and lead to a series of cellular and molecular changes that result in an acute migraine attack. However, as attractive as this explanation may seem, the information provided by migraineurs as well as the existing objective data from numerous clinical trials do not exclude the possibility that the sequence of events is happening exactly in the opposite direction. It is well known that the pathophysiologic phenomenon of a migraine attack starts well before the onset of the pain phase [11]. In this context, premonitory symptoms, such as food cravings, yawning and alterations in the sleep wake cycle, have been reported to precede the pain phase of a migraine attack by up to 72 hours. Therefore, it may be postulated, that an altered brain state, that probably involves a transient inadequate function of central modulating structures such as the hypothalamus, may increase for example the feeling of hunger thereby inducing the observed food cravings, maybe even the craving for specific foods that are then misinterpreted as the initial cause of the migraine attack. The same may apply for external factors such as specific meteorological variables. In this case, during the early phases of a migraine attack, long before the pain starts, migraineurs perceive weather changes more intensely as a result of an enhanced neuronal susceptibility or even sensitization. Presently, it is not possible to conclude with certainty which of the two mechanisms is the pathophysiologic basis of the commonly reported connection between migraine and the environment. Even the possibility that both mechanisms coexist could be conceivable. However, what can be concluded is that the relationship between environmental factors and migraine appears to be far more complex than initially assumed. The type and extent of this relationship may also vary substantially among migraineurs. The pathophysiologic complexity is reflected in the discrepancy between migraineurs' clinical reports that highly suggest such a relationship and objective data of clinical trials that deliver inconclusive results. Given the amount of affected patients, the inconclusive results are probably the result of migraine heterogeneity, lack of pathophysiological understanding or methodological shortcomings in trial design, rather than a common misperception of millions of migraineurs. Here, we review the clinical and pathophysiological facts that support or refute a correlation between certain environmental stimuli and the occurrence of migraine attacks. We also highlight the methodological difficulties of investigating the link between environmental factors and migraine. In 1960, Selby and Lance published a seminal observational study revealing that 25 % of migraineurs identified foods as triggers for their attacks [13]. Most recently, in a large retrospective study, Kelman evaluated 1,207 patients with migraine and confirmed that one out of four migraineurs reported food as a precipitant of their acute migraine attacks [1]. fetched_contents.text: Migraine attack triggers There are many factors that may trigger migraine attacks. We look at some of the most common migraine triggers here. About migraine triggers A migraine trigger is something that seems to cause or worsen a migraine attack. If you have migraine, you may be keen to try and identify your triggers as a way to help manage your migraine. But this isn’t always easy. Many people don’t have any obvious triggers, and some – such as weather changes – can’t be controlled. Although trying to avoid known triggers can be helpful for some people, focusing on this too much can cause more harm than good. We have more information on identifying and managing triggers at the end of the page. Migraine threshold theory When you live with migraine, it can feel like almost anything might trigger an attack. In reality, only a few factors make a significant difference to your risk of getting an attack on their own. It’s more likely to be a combination of several things that leads to a migraine attack. For example, you may find that you are more likely to have migraine attacks when you: * have not eaten or skipped meals * have not had much sleep * are under a lot of stress. While one of these things on its own may be less likely to lead to a migraine attack, two or three together may push you over the threshold for an attack. This is known as the ‘threshold theory’. A threshold is a level when something starts to happen – like a migraine attack. Your threshold may shift up or down, making you more or less sensitive to an attack at different times. This can be influenced by things like hormonal changes and illness. Migraine triggers and warning signs Sometimes, what you think is a migraine trigger may actually be an early symptom of a migraine attack. This is known as the ‘prodrome’ or ‘warning’ stage of a migraine attack. During this stage, you may get symptoms such as mood changes, neck stiffness or pain, and cravings for certain foods. You may also notice you’re more sensitive to light, sound or smells. It can be easy to mistake these warning signs for triggers. For example: * if you eat chocolate to satisfy a craving in the prodrome stage, you may think that chocolate is a trigger * if you are more sensitive to light in the warning stage, you might think bright lights are a trigger * if you have neck pain or stiffness as a prodrome symptom, you might think this is a trigger. If you believe something to be a trigger when it’s not, you might try to avoid it for no reason. But if you know that something is a warning sign, it could help you to spot an attack early and get the treatment you need sooner. This may reduce how much impact the migraine attack has. It’s not easy to tell whether something is a warning sign or a trigger. But keeping a diary may help. We have more information on this below. Common migraine triggers Below we list some of the most commonly-reported migraine triggers. It’s important to bear in mind that triggers can be different for everyone. You may not have any of the triggers listed here, or you may have identified different triggers to those listed. Many people find it’s a change in their usual routine that triggers a migraine attack. This relates to many of the factors below, including sleep patterns, mealtimes, caffeine and stress. Migraine is frequently linked to change in hormone levels, particularly oestrogen. If you have periods, you may find you are more likely to have migraine attacks around the start of your period. This is known as menstrual migraine. Rapid changes in your hormone levels can also trigger migraine attacks in the lead up to menopause. But after menopause, migraine attacks may become less severe and less frequent. Stress is one of the most commonly-reported triggers for migraine attacks. This is thought to be down to a hormone that you produce when you’re stressed, which may make migraine attacks more likely. Some people find that their migraine attacks start when they stop feeling stressed, and stress hormones decline. They may find that they are more likely to have migraine attacks at a weekend or on holiday, when they come to relax. This is sometimes called a ‘let-down migraine’. Many people report lack of sleep as a migraine attack trigger. Sleep deprivation may have a direct effect on the migraine pathway in the brain. Some people find that having more sleep than usual, for example having a lie-in on a weekend, can increase the risk of a migraine attack. A change in your usual sleep patterns can have the same effect. Good sleep hygiene, including keeping to regular bedtimes and wake times, may help. Fasting (not eating) or missing meals causes a drop in your blood sugar levels. Many people find migraine attacks can become more frequent and more severe after a period without eating. Making sure you stick to regular mealtimes and not going too long between meals may help. We have more information on healthy eating for migraine on our Migraine and diet page. Having too much caffeine can lead to a migraine attack for some people. However, cutting out caffeine suddenly can also trigger migraine attacks. If you think caffeine may be a trigger, it’s best to try and gradually cut down the amount you have, rather than stopping suddenly. Caffeine is in tea, coffee and cola, as well as chocolate and some over-the-counter painkillers. Many people find alcohol to be a migraine trigger. Red wine is the most common alcoholic drink reported as trigger. If alcohol does affect you this way, it may not happen every time you drink. It can depend on how much you have drunk, and what other factors may be present – such as if you are tired or stressed. Many people with migraine identify certain foods as migraine attack triggers. Common examples include chocolate, dairy, and foods containing tyramine, monosodium glutamate (MSG) and nitrates. However, there is a lack of evidence to support food triggers for migraine. Environmental factors are commonly reported as migraine triggers, but the evidence base is mixed: patients and clinicians often report them strongly, yet systematic reviews note conflicting clinical results and methodological limitations [N1-F2]. The most consistently linked environmental triggers are light, sounds, and weather/climate changes, with less consistent or weaker evidence for air quality in the provided evidence.

Specific environmental triggers most consistently linked to migraines:
- **Light sensitivity** is repeatedly cited as a trigger. Migraineurs often report bright or flickering lights, and the evidence notes that migraine sufferers may be more sensitive to light generally [N1-R5]. The review also states that light is among the environmental stimuli commonly reported as triggering or aggravating migraine attacks [N1-F2].
- **Sounds/soundsensitivity** are also commonly reported. The same review identifies exposure to sounds as a factor that migraineurs report as triggering or aggravating migraine attacks [N1-F2]. The patient-oriented source similarly notes that non-dietary triggers include environmental factors and that sound is a known migraine trigger [N3-F3].
- **Weather and climate changes** are a major reported environmental trigger. The review explicitly mentions meteorologic or atmospheric changes as factors migraineurs commonly report [N1-F2]. The National Headache Foundation similarly notes that climate or weather changes, such as changes in humidity or temperature, can trigger migraine attacks [N1-R2]. The evidence base for weather is stronger in patient reports than in objective clinical studies, which is a recurring theme in the review [N1-F2].
- **Sleep disturbance, stress, and circadian rhythm disruption** are important, but they are not air quality-related. The review and patient-oriented source both emphasize that sleep deprivation, lack of sleep, stress, and irregular sleep patterns can increase migraine risk [N1-F2][N3-F3]. The circadian rhythm literature adds that migraine is linked to circadian disruptions and morning attack peaks, with circadian variations in pain sensitivity and hypothalamic involvement [N4-R2]. This is relevant to environmental exposure in the sense that shifts in daily routine or irregular sleep can be seen as environmental stressors, but the evidence provided does not specifically support air quality as a strong trigger [N4-R2][N4-R5].

How weather, light, noise, and air quality may contribute:
- **Weather/climate changes** are likely to contribute through perceived sensitivity rather than a direct causal mechanism. The review explains that migraineurs may perceive weather changes more intensely during the early phases of a migraine attack because of heightened neuronal susceptibility or sensitization [N1-F2]. The patient source also notes that weather changes are difficult to control and that people may mistake warning signs for triggers [N3-F3].
- **Light** contributes by increasing sensitivity in migraineurs, who may be more sensitive to light generally. The review explicitly states that exposure to light is among the environmental stimuli that migraineurs report as triggering or aggravating attacks [N1-F2]. The patient-oriented source similarly notes that sensitivity to light can be an early symptom and that bright lights may be reported as a trigger [N3-F3].
- **Noise** contributes by acting as a sensory trigger. The review identifies sounds as a factor that migraineurs report as triggering or aggravating attacks [N1-F2], and the patient source notes that sound is one of the commonly-reported triggers [N3-F3].
- **Air quality** is not strongly supported in the provided evidence. The evidence set here does not provide direct evidence that air quality is a consistently linked trigger. The closest related evidence is on sleep, stress, circadian rhythm, and weather, not on air pollutants or air quality [N1-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Strength of evidence for each trigger:
- **Strongest evidence:** Light and sounds are repeatedly reported and are part of the broad clinical discussion in the review [N1-F2]. Weather changes are also strongly reported in patient and patient-oriented sources, but the evidence is still mixed and not fully confirmed by objective clinical studies [N1-R2][N1-F2].
- **Moderate to mixed evidence:** Sleep disturbance, stress, and circadian rhythm disruption are supported by both the migraine trigger review and the sleep/circadian literature, but they are not “environmental” in the narrow sense of air quality or outdoor conditions [N1-F2][N4-R2][N4-R5]. The review explicitly warns that most clinical studies have shown conflicting results and that natural experimentation is not reliable for identifying triggers [N1-F2].
- **Weaker evidence:** Air quality is not supported in the provided evidence. The evidence set here does not include direct studies linking air quality to migraine, so any recommendation about air quality should be considered tentative or outside the current evidence base [N1-F2][N4-R2].

Overall, the evidence supports a practical conclusion: environmental triggers are real and commonly reported, but the strongest supported triggers are light, sounds, and weather changes, while air quality is not strongly established in the provided sources [N1-F2][N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F3][N4-R2].

A patient can take several practical steps to avoid environmental migraine triggers. The evidence base emphasizes keeping a trigger diary, making lifestyle/environment changes that are realistic, and knowing when to seek specialist help if triggers remain unclear or persistent.

How to keep a trigger diary and interpret it:
- The most direct evidence is that keeping a diary is a standard method for identifying triggers. The patient-oriented source states, “Keeping a diary may also show that some things you believed to be triggers may not be triggers at all” [N3-F3]. It also notes that a diary can help identify triggers and monitor changes in frequency and severity [N3-F3].
- The review also cautions that natural experimentation is not reliable for identifying triggers and suggests that formal experimentation or diary studies using advanced statistical modeling may be necessary [N1-F2]. This means a diary should not be used as a simple “yes/no” list of triggers, but as a tool to detect patterns over time.
- The threshold theory adds that only a few factors may matter on their own, but combinations of several things may push someone over the threshold for an attack [N3-F3]. So the diary should be interpreted in context: what appears to be a trigger may actually be a warning sign or a combination of factors, including sleep, stress, and routine changes.

Lifestyle and environment changes that are actionable and realistic:
- **Sleep hygiene improvements** are a highly actionable change. The patient-oriented source explicitly states that improving sleep hygiene is one of the most frequently discussed aspects, and the review evidence shows that sleep disturbance is a major reported migraine trigger [N3-F3][N1-F2]. Practical steps include keeping regular bedtimes and wake times, avoiding excessive sleep or irregular sleep patterns, and managing sleep deprivation [N1-F2][N3-F3].
- **Stress management techniques** are also actionable. The review evidence notes that stress is one of the most commonly-reported triggers [N1-F2], and the lifestyle source says stress management is a frequently discussed intervention [N3-R2]. Realistic strategies include identifying stressors, practicing relaxation techniques, and addressing stress in daily life rather than trying to eliminate it completely.
- **Regular mealtimes and avoiding fasting** are practical. The patient-oriented source says missing meals can lower blood sugar and increase migraine frequency and severity, so regular eating is advised [N3-F3]. It also notes that caffeine and alcohol can be triggers for some people, and that caffeine should be reduced gradually rather than abruptly [N3-F3].
- **Reducing exposure to known triggers** is realistic where possible. For light sensitivity, using sunglasses, avoiding bright or flickering lights, and staying in dimmer environments can help. For sounds, reducing exposure to loud noises or using ear protection when needed may help [N1-R5][N3-F3]. For weather/climate changes, avoiding travel or outdoor exposure during extreme weather may be practical, though the evidence does not support air quality as a strong trigger [N1-R2][N1-F2].
- **Keeping a routine** is a realistic change. The patient-oriented source notes that changes in routine are often associated with migraine attacks and that maintaining regular sleep, mealtimes, and caffeine use can help [N3-F3].

When to seek specialist help if triggers are unclear or persistent:
- If a patient finds that triggers remain unclear after careful diary use, specialist referral is indicated. The evidence from the diagnostic/management source says that migraine diagnosis can be challenging and that specialist guidance is relevant to headache disorders [N6-R3]. The review also notes that the relationship between environmental factors and migraine is complex and may vary substantially among individuals [N1-F2], so persistent or unclear triggers may point to a need for more expert assessment.
- Specialist help is also indicated if migraine is frequent or if self-management does not sufficiently reduce attacks. The evidence on repetitive migraines and diagnostic workup shows that specialists may be needed to optimize diagnosis and treatment [N2][N6]. The patient-oriented source also advises that if someone believes something is a trigger when it is not, they may benefit from specialist help to distinguish warning signs from true triggers [N3-F3].
- The specialist-level guidance in the provided evidence supports referral when headaches are difficult to classify or when the pattern suggests a more complex disorder. The ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria and specialist referral guidance indicate that headache diagnosis can be challenging and that specialist assessment is appropriate when the diagnosis is uncertain or when treatment is not responding well [N2-R1][N6-R3]. This means that specialist help is appropriate when triggers are unclear, when attacks are persistent, or when the patient wants to explore more targeted management options.

Which diagnostic criteria or specialist assessments are relevant:
- The ICHD-3 criteria are central to migraine diagnosis. The ICHD-3 source provides the official classification system and states that headache diagnosis can be challenging because of diverse underlying causes and subjective pain perception [N2-R4][N2-F1]. - The evidence also highlights that headache diagnosis is not straightforward because migraine can overlap with other headache disorders, and some headaches may be secondary or medication overuse-related [N2-R4][N2-F1]. This means specialist assessment is especially relevant when distinguishing migraine from other headaches, including secondary headaches or medication-related headaches.

What treatment options are supported for frequent migraines:
- **Lifestyle and trigger management** are foundational. The evidence supports keeping a trigger diary, improving sleep hygiene, managing stress, and maintaining regular mealtimes [N3-F3][N3-R2]. These are considered part of the broader treatment approach rather than standalone cures.

- **Prophylaxis is indicated when migraines are frequent enough to affect quality of life.** The evidence supports starting prophylaxis for patients with frequent migraine attacks, with a low starting dose and gradual titration [N5-R1]. The preventive migraine treatment source also states that preventive measures should be used when migraine is present [N5-R2].

## Can migraines be caused by the environment? Yes, but the evidence is mixed

The short answer is: **yes, environmental factors are commonly reported as migraine triggers**, but the evidence is not always strong or conclusive. Migraineurs often report that things like **light, sounds, weather changes, and sleep disturbance** can trigger or worsen attacks [N1-F2][N1-R2][N1-R5][N3-F3]. However, the review evidence also notes that **most clinical studies have shown conflicting results** and that natural experimentation is not reliable for identifying triggers [N1-F2]. So, environmental factors are real and important in many people’s experience, but they are not the only cause, and not all reported triggers have strong scientific support [N1-F2].

## Which environmental factors are most likely to matter?

### 1. **Light sensitivity**
This is one of the most consistently reported triggers. Migraine sufferers often report bright or flickering lights, and the evidence says that exposure to light is among the environmental stimuli that migraineurs commonly report as triggering or aggravating attacks [N1-F2][N1-R5]. The patient-oriented source also notes that sensitivity to light can be an early warning sign and that bright lights may be reported as a trigger [N3-F3].

### 2. **Sounds/sound sensitivity**
Sounds are also commonly reported as triggers. The review identifies exposure to sounds as a factor that migraineurs report as triggering or aggravating attacks [N1-F2]. The patient source similarly notes that sound is one of the commonly-reported triggers [N3-F3].

### 3. **Weather and climate changes**
Weather changes are a major reported environmental trigger. The review explicitly mentions meteorologic or atmospheric changes as factors migraineurs commonly report [N1-F2]. The National Headache Foundation also notes that climate or weather changes, such as changes in humidity or temperature, can trigger migraine attacks [N1-R2]. The evidence is stronger in patient reports than in objective clinical studies, so weather changes are plausible but not definitively proven for everyone [N1-F2].

### 4. **Sleep disturbance, stress, and circadian rhythm disruption**
These are important contributors, but they are more broadly related to migraine vulnerability than to a specific “environmental” trigger. The evidence shows that sleep disturbance, stress, and irregular sleep patterns are major reported migraine triggers [N1-F2][N3-F3]. Circadian rhythm disruption is also linked to migraine, with studies showing links to morning attack peaks, circadian variations in pain sensitivity, and hypothalamic involvement [N4-R2][N4-R5]. So these are important environmental-style stressors in the sense that they can be influenced by daily routine or external demands, but the evidence here does not specifically support air quality as a strong trigger [N1-F2][N4-R2].

### 5. **Air quality**
In the evidence provided, **air quality is not strongly supported** as a consistently linked trigger. The evidence set here does not include direct studies linking air quality to migraine, so any recommendation about air quality should be considered tentative or outside the current evidence base [N1-F2][N4-R2].

## What to do next: practical steps to manage environmental triggers

### 1. Keep a migraine diary and interpret it carefully
The evidence says keeping a diary is one of the best ways to identify triggers [N3-F3]. The review also cautions that natural experimentation is not reliable and that formal experimentation or diary studies using advanced statistical modeling may be necessary [N1-F2]. So, the diary should be used as a pattern-finding tool rather than a simple “yes/no” checklist.

The threshold theory adds that only a few factors may matter on their own, but combinations of several things may push someone over the threshold for an attack [N3-F3]. That means what looks like a trigger may actually be a warning sign or part of a broader pattern. For example, light sensitivity, neck pain, or mood changes may be early symptoms of an attack rather than the direct cause [N3-F3].

### 2. Make realistic lifestyle and environment changes
The evidence supports several practical changes that are actionable and realistic:

- **Improve sleep hygiene:** Keep regular bedtimes and wake times, avoid excessive sleep, and manage sleep deprivation [N1-F2][N3-F3].
- **Manage stress:** Stress management techniques are frequently discussed in the evidence, and stress is one of the most commonly-reported triggers [N1-F2][N3-R2].
- **Maintain regular mealtimes:** Missing meals or fasting can lower blood sugar and increase migraine frequency and severity, so regular eating is advised [N3-F3].
- **Reduce exposure to known triggers:** Where possible, avoid bright or flickering lights, reduce loud noises, and avoid travel or outdoor exposure during extreme weather [N1-R5][N1-R2][N3-F3].

### 3. Know when to seek specialist help
If your triggers remain unclear or if migraines are persistent, specialist help is appropriate. The evidence shows that migraine diagnosis can be challenging and that specialist assessment is needed when headaches are difficult to classify or when the diagnosis is uncertain [N2-R4][N6-R3]. The ICHD-3 criteria and specialist referral guidance also indicate that headache diagnosis is not always straightforward, and specialist evaluation is appropriate when the diagnosis is pending confirmation during early follow-up [N2-R1][N6-R3].

If self-management does not sufficiently reduce attacks, specialist referral is especially important. The evidence supports specialist assessment when migraines are frequent, persistent, or refractory, and it also indicates that referred patient profiles should be optimized for diagnostic and referral approaches [N6-R5].

## What medical evaluation and treatment options are appropriate for repetitive migraines?

### 1. Diagnostic evaluation
The ICHD-3 criteria are central to migraine diagnosis [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that headache diagnosis can be challenging because of diverse underlying causes and subjective pain perception [N2-R4]. Specialists distinguish migraine from other headache disorders by using the ICHD-3 criteria and by considering overlapping conditions and secondary causes [N2-F1][N2-R4].

### 2. Treatment options for frequent migraines
The evidence supports a combination of lifestyle/trigger management and medication-based prophylaxis:

- **Lifestyle and trigger management** are foundational. Keeping a diary, improving sleep hygiene, managing stress, and maintaining regular mealtimes are all recommended [N3-F3][N3-R2].
- **Preventive medication** is supported for frequent migraines. The evidence includes information on migraine prophylaxis, including starting at a low dose and gradually titrating medication [N5-R1]. Preventive medicines are also described as taken regularly to help stop migraine attacks developing [N5-R5].
- **Specialist assessment** is appropriate when migraines are frequent enough to affect quality of life [N5-R2]. The evidence also supports specialist referral when headaches are difficult to classify or when treatment is not responding well [N6-R3].

### 3. When prophylaxis or specialist referral is indicated
Prophylaxis is indicated when migraines are frequent and bothersome enough to warrant regular preventive treatment [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Specialist referral is indicated when diagnosis is uncertain, when attacks are persistent, or when self-management is insufficient [N6-R3]. Specialist referral is especially important for complex or refractory migraines, and the evidence supports multidisciplinary headache centers or specialist settings when headaches are difficult to classify or not responding well [N6-R5].

## What specialists recommend about triggers and management

Specialist guidance says that migraine diagnosis is not always straightforward [N2-R4]. Specialists distinguish migraine from other headache disorders using the ICHD-3 criteria and by considering overlapping conditions and secondary causes [N2-F1]. They also caution that trigger identification is not always reliable and that structured diary keeping is more reliable than natural experimentation [N1-F2][N3-F3].

Specialist recommendations also support distinguishing warning signs from true triggers. The patient-oriented source explains that prodromal symptoms such as mood changes, neck stiffness, cravings, and light sensitivity may be mistaken for triggers [N3-F3]. Specialist-level thinking likely includes using that distinction to improve early intervention.

For refractory or complex migraines, specialist settings such as neurology clinics, headache specialist clinics, or multidisciplinary headache centers are most appropriate [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Referral to a headache specialist is especially indicated when migraines are frequent, persistent, or difficult to classify [N2-R4][N6-R3].

## Bottom line

Yes, **environmental factors can play a role in migraines**, but the evidence is mixed: **light, sounds, and weather changes are the most consistently reported triggers**, while air quality is not strongly supported in the provided evidence [N1-F2][N1-R5][N1-R2][N3-F3]. The best approach is:

1. **Keep a migraine diary** to identify patterns and distinguish warning signs from true triggers [N3-F3][N1-F2].
2. **Make realistic lifestyle/environment changes** such as improving sleep, managing stress, keeping regular mealtimes, and reducing exposure to known triggers [N3-F3][N3-R2].
3. **Seek specialist help if triggers remain unclear or if migraines are persistent** [N2-R4][N6-R3].
4. **Consider prophylactic treatment** when migraines are frequent enough to interfere with daily life [N5-R1][N5-R2].
